quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "around" ends in /d/ and "your" begins with a /j/ sound. What single new consonant do the two combine into?
quests.explanation: When /d/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two often fuse into a single new consonant. In "around your", /d/ + /j/ becomes /dʒ/ — a completely different sound from either original.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen closely at the boundary of "last" and "call" — count the consonants stacking up. Does the /t/ still make it into the sentence?
quests.explanation: In fast, connected speech, a /t/ wedged between consonants almost always disappears. That's what you'll hear in "last call" — the /t/ goes silent.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Instead of hearing /d/ and /j/ separately between "attend" and "your", listen for one fused sound. What is it?
quests.explanation: This is coalescent assimilation: two adjacent sounds merge into a third sound that resembles neither one alone. Here, /d/ and /j/ combine into /dʒ/ in "attend your".
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "seven". With a velar consonant starting "cups" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /n/ ending "seven" to a velar sound, the mouth compromises: /n/ becomes /ŋ/, matching the velar consonant that opens "cups".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "gift card" naturally, without pausing between the words. Is the /t/ audible, or does it disappear into the next consonant?
quests.explanation: Elision removes a sound completely rather than merely blending it. Here the /t/ vanishes from "gift" so the phrase moves directly into "card".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "data" has no letter for /r/ anywhere at its end. So if you hear a /r/ before "entry", where does it actually come from?
quests.explanation: English avoids putting two vowel sounds directly next to each other, so speakers insert a small linking sound to bridge them. Since "data" has no /r/ in its spelling, this /r/ is intrusive — added purely for smoothness, not because it's really part of "data" or "entry".
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This pair, "round trip", creates a tricky consonant sequence. Which sound do fluent speakers simplify away — and is it really gone, or just quieter?
quests.explanation: Speakers naturally avoid three consonants in a row, so the /d/ is dropped rather than forced through. That's why "round trip" sounds smoother without it.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Both "comma" and "and" end and begin with vowel sounds. Listen for an extra consonant sound that sneaks in between them.
quests.explanation: This is intrusion: a sound appears between two vowels even though it isn't written anywhere. In "comma and", an intrusive /r/ bridges the gap, purely to avoid an awkward vowel collision.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "ten kilos" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /n/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /n/ rarely stays /n/ before a velar sound — it assimilates to /ŋ/, which is exactly what you hear in "ten kilos".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Fluent speech avoids awkward consonant pile-ups. Where exactly does that simplification happen in "act fast"?
quests.explanation: This cluster is simplified by deleting the /t/ altogether — not weakening it, not shifting it, just leaving it out — which is the defining feature of elision in "act fast".
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The tongue is already anticipating "passengers"'s bilabial sound before it even finishes "ten". What happens to /n/ as a result?
quests.explanation: The change from /n/ to /m/ at the end of "ten" happens because the following bilabial consonant in "passengers" pulls the place of articulation to match. Nothing is lost here, just reshaped.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "left" alone, then "behind" alone — both consonants are clear. Now blend them at speed. What happens to the /t/ in between?
quests.explanation: Notice that nothing replaces the /t/ — it isn't weakened or swapped for another sound, it's simply omitted. That full deletion is what separates elision from assimilation in "left behind".
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "drama unfolds" without a pause. Two vowel sounds are about to collide — what does English insert to smooth the transition?
quests.explanation: Because "drama" ends in a vowel and "unfolds" begins with one, English speakers instinctively insert /r/ between them. It's not in the spelling of either word — it's added on the fly to keep the speech flowing.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Between "not" and "bad" sits a consonant under pressure to match its neighbor. What does it become?
quests.explanation: This pairing is a classic assimilation example: the /t/ ending "not" adopts the bilabial quality of the sound in "bad", surfacing as /p/ in natural, connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "before" already has a written 'r' at the end — normally silent before a pause, but what happens to it right before the vowel that opens "everyone"?
quests.explanation: "before" ends in a written 'r' that's silent in isolation (in non-rhotic pronunciation) but reappears whenever a vowel follows. Because "everyone" begins with a vowel, the /r/ resurfaces — this is linking /r/, not intrusion, since the letter is genuinely there in "before".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "organize your" quickly and casually. The /z/ and the /j/ in "your" don't stay separate — what do they merge into?
quests.explanation: Rather than two separate consonants, connected speech blends /z/ and /j/ into /ʒ/. That's why "organize your" sounds like one smooth unit rather than two words bumping together.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling of "camera" before "or" — does it end in a letter that would predict a /r/ sound? If not, where's that /r/ actually coming from?
quests.explanation: Unlike linking, where the connecting sound is already written into the word, this /r/ in "camera or" comes from nowhere in the spelling. That's exactly what makes it intrusive rather than a genuine linking sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This isn't a case of a sound vanishing from "ten" — it's still there, just different. What does /n/ turn into before the bilabial sound in "branches"?
quests.explanation: Notice that the /n/ ending "ten" isn't deleted the way it would be in elision — it survives, just transformed into /m/ to match the bilabial sound beginning "branches".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A stop consonant squeezed between two other consonants rarely survives in fast speech. Listen for the /d/ in "wild guess" — is it there?
quests.explanation: Consonant clusters like this one are common at word boundaries in English, and the middle stop is almost always the casualty. The /d/ drops out of "wild guess" for exactly that reason.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "spend time" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /d/ in "spend" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /d/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "spend time", the /d/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Vowel sounds rarely bump directly into each other in fluent English. What extra sound bridges "banana" and "ice" here?
quests.explanation: Two vowel sounds meeting head-on is hard to say smoothly, so speakers add /r/ as a natural bridge. You'll hear it in "banana ice", even though neither word's spelling contains it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "find" and "your": /d/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /d/ and /j/ become /dʒ/ in "find your" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two consonants become one here. Focus on where "amaze" ends and "your" begins — what's the resulting blended sound?
quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /z/ meets a "you"-type word. In "amaze your", the result is /ʒ/, not /z/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Rather than pronouncing /s/ then /j/ separately, fluent speakers coalesce them. What do you actually hear in "discuss your"?
quests.explanation: Notice that neither the original /s/ nor /j/ survives on its own — they combine into /ʃ/. That fusion is what makes "discuss your" sound natural and fast.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen at natural speed: does "won't you" keep two distinct consonant sounds at the boundary, or blend them into a new one?
quests.explanation: In relaxed, natural speech, /t/ and /j/ rarely stay separate at a word boundary like this one. They coalesce into /tʃ/, exactly as in "won't you".
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "four o'clock" naturally. That final 'r' in "four", usually silent, resurfaces here — why, do you think?
quests.explanation: This is linking, not intrusion, because the 'r' is already written into "four". It stays silent before a pause or consonant but comes back to life right before the vowel that opens "o'clock".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: The /t/ at the end of "that" is about to meet a velar sound in "car". Does it hold firm, or shift to match?
quests.explanation: Before a velar consonant, /t/ commonly shifts to match its place of articulation. In "that car", /t/ becomes /k/ — the sound itself changes, it doesn't disappear.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation changes a sound's place of articulation to match its neighbor — /t/, /d/, and /n/ are the sounds most commonly affected before bilabial or velar consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's no /r/ anywhere in the spelling of "draw". Yet something links it to the vowel that opens "a" — what is it?
quests.explanation: This inserted /r/ has no basis in spelling — it exists purely to smooth the vowel-to-vowel transition between "draw" and "a". That's the hallmark of intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "first" and "class". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /t/ in "first class" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen carefully between "agenda" and "ahead". An unwritten sound appears purely to ease the vowel-to-vowel transition. Which one?
quests.explanation: Native speakers automatically fill the gap between two vowel sounds with /r/, even when there's no letter to justify it. "agenda ahead" is a clear example of this intrusive sound.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.
